{{Short description|Mathematical technique}}
{{Distinguish|Cross product}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[elementary arithmetic]] and [[elementary algebra]], given an equation between two [[Fraction (mathematics)|fractions]] or [[rational fraction|rational expressions]], one can '''cross-multiply''' to simplify the equation or determine the value of a variable.

The method is also occasionally known as the "cross your heart" method because lines resembling a heart outline can be drawn to remember which things to multiply together.

Given an equation like

<math display="block">\frac a b = \frac c d,</math>

where {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|d}} are not zero, one can cross-multiply to get

<math display="block">ad = bc \quad \text{or} \quad a = \frac{bc}d.</math>

In [[Euclidean geometry]] the same calculation can be achieved by considering the [[ratio]]s as those of [[similar triangle]]s.

== Procedure ==
In practice, the method of cross-multiplying means that we multiply the numerator of each (or one) side by the denominator of the other side, effectively crossing the terms over:

<math display="block">\frac a b \nwarrow \frac c d, \quad \frac a b \nearrow \frac c d.</math>

The mathematical justification for the method is from the following longer mathematical procedure. If we start with the basic equation

<math display="block">\frac a b = \frac c d,</math>

we can multiply the terms on each side by the same number, and the terms will remain equal. Therefore, if we multiply the fraction on each side by the product of the denominators of both sides—{{mvar|bd}}—we get

<math display="block">\frac a b \times bd = \frac c d \times bd.</math>

We can reduce the fractions to lowest terms by noting that the two occurrences of {{mvar|b}} on the left-hand side cancel, as do the two occurrences of {{mvar|d}} on the right-hand side, leaving

<math display="block">ad = bc,</math>

and we can divide both sides of the equation by any of the elements—in this case we will use {{mvar|d}}—getting

<math display="block">a = \frac{bc}d.</math>

Another justification of cross-multiplication is as follows. Starting with the given equation

<math display="block">\frac a b = \frac c d,</math>

multiply by {{math|{{sfrac|''d''|''d''}}}} = 1 on the left and by {{math|{{sfrac|''b''|''b''}}}} = 1 on the right, getting

<math display="block">\frac a b \times \frac d d = \frac c d \times \frac b b,</math>

and so

<math display="block">\frac{ad}{bd} = \frac{cb}{db}.</math>

Cancel the common denominator {{mvar|bd}} = {{mvar|db}}, leaving

<math display="block">ad = cb.</math>

Each step in these procedures is based on a single, fundamental property of [[equation]]s. Cross-multiplication is a shortcut, an easily understandable procedure that can be taught to students.

== Use ==
This is a common procedure in mathematics, used to reduce fractions or calculate a value for a given variable in a fraction. If we have an equation

<math display="block">\frac x b = \frac c d,</math>

where {{mvar|x}} is a variable we are interested in solving for, we can use cross-multiplication to determine that

<math display="block">x = \frac{bc}d.</math>

For example, suppose we want to know how far a car will travel in 7&nbsp;hours, if we know that its speed is constant and that it already travelled 90&nbsp;miles in the last 3&nbsp;hours. Converting the word problem into ratios, we get

<math display="block">\frac x{7\ \text{hours}} = \frac{90\ \text{miles}} {3\ \text{hours}}.</math>

Cross-multiplying yields

<math display="block">x = \frac{7\ \text{hours} \times 90\ \text{miles}}{3\ \text{hours}},</math>

and so

<math display="block">x = 210\ \text{miles}.</math>

'''Alternate solution'''

'''{{sfrac|90miles|3hours}}=30mph'''

'''So, 30mph×7hours=210miles.'''

Note that even simple equations like

<math display="block">a = \frac{x}{d}</math>

are solved using cross-multiplication, since the missing {{mvar|b}} term is implicitly equal to 1:

<math display="block">\frac a 1 = \frac x d.</math>

Any equation containing fractions or rational expressions can be simplified by multiplying both sides by the [[least common denominator]]. This step is called ''[[clearing fractions]]''.


== Rule of three ==

The '''rule of three'''<ref>This was sometimes also referred to as the '''golden rule''', though that usage is rare compared to other uses of [[Golden Rule]]. See {{cite book |author=E. Cobham Brewer |authorlink=E. Cobham Brewer |title=Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable |location=Philadelphia |publisher=Henry Altemus |year=1898 |chapter=Golden Rule |chapter-url=http://www.bartleby.com/81/7351.html}}</ref> was a historical shorthand version for a particular form of cross-multiplication that could be taught to students by rote. It was considered the height of [[Thirteen Colonies|Colonial]] maths education<ref>{{cite book |title=Handbook on the History of Mathematics Education |chapter=Mathematics Education in America in the Premodern Period |author=[[Ubiratan D'Ambrósio]] |author2=[[Joseph W. Dauben]] |author3=[[Karen Hunger Parshall]] |editor=Alexander Karp |editor2=Gert Schubring |page=177 |publisher=Springer Science |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4614-9155-2}}</ref> and still figures in the French national curriculum for secondary education,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://eduscol.education.fr/cid47414/pilier-3.html |title=Socle de connaissances, pilier 3 |publisher=French ministry of education |date=30 December 2012  |access-date=24 September 2015}}</ref> and in the primary education curriculum of Spain.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=BOE-A-2014-2222 |title=Real Decreto 126/2014, de 28 de febrero, por el que se establece el currículo básico de la Educación Primaria. |publisher=Ministerio de Educación, Cultura y Deporte |date=28 February 2014 |pages=19349–19420 |access-date=10 May 2022}}</ref>

For an equation of the form

<math display="block">\frac a b = \frac c x,</math>

where the variable to be evaluated is in the right-hand denominator, the rule of three states that

<math display="block">x = \frac{bc}a.</math>

In this context, {{mvar|a}} is referred to as the ''extreme'' of the proportion, and {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|c}} are called the ''means''.

This rule was already known to Chinese mathematicians prior to the 2nd century CE,<ref>{{cite book |author1=Shen Kangshen |author2=John N. Crossley |author3=Anthony W.-C. Lun |title=The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: Companion and Commentary |location=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1999}}</ref> though it was not used in Europe until much later.

[[Cocker's Arithmetick]], the premier textbook in the 17th century, introduces its discussion of the rule of three<ref>{{cite book |author=Edward Cocker |title=Cocker's Arithmetick |date=1702 |location=London |publisher=John Hawkins |page=[https://archive.org/details/cockersarithmet00cockgoog/page/n117 103] |url=https://archive.org/details/cockersarithmet00cockgoog}}</ref> with the problem "If 4&nbsp;yards of cloth cost 12&nbsp;shillings, what will 6&nbsp;yards cost at that rate?" The rule of three gives the answer to this problem directly; whereas in modern arithmetic, we would solve it by introducing a variable {{mvar|x}} to stand for the cost of 6&nbsp;yards of cloth, writing down the equation

<math display="block">\frac{4\ \text{yards}}{12\ \text{shillings}} = \frac{6\ \text{yards}}{x}</math>

and then using cross-multiplication to calculate {{mvar|x}}:

<math display="block">x = \frac{12\ \text{shillings} \times 6\ \text{yards}}{4\ \text{yards}} = 18\ \text{shillings}.</math>

An anonymous manuscript dated 1570<ref>Concise Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, 1964.</ref> said:
"Multiplication is vexation, / Division is as bad; / The Rule of three doth puzzle me, / And Practice drives me mad."

[[Charles Darwin]] refers to his use of the rule of three in estimating the number of species in a newly discerned genus.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ariew |first1=André |title=Charles Darwin as a statistical thinker |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science |date=2022 |volume=95 |pages=215–223 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsa.2022.08.005 |pmid=36113233 |s2cid=252246047 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.shpsa.2022.08.005|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In a letter to [[William Darwin Fox]] in 1855, Charles Darwin declared “I have no faith in anything short of actual measurement and the Rule of Three.”<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stigler |first1=Stephen M |title=The Seven Pillars of Statistical Wisdom |date=March 7, 2016 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0674088917 |edition=Illustrated}}</ref> [[Karl Pearson]] adopted this declaration as the motto of his newly founded journal [[Biometrika]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stigler |first1=Stephen M |title=The Seven Pillars of Statistical Wisdom |date=March 7, 2016 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0674088917 |edition=Illustrated}}</ref>
=== Double rule of three ===

An extension to the rule of three was the '''double rule of three''', which involved finding an unknown value where five rather than three other values are known.

An example of such a problem might be ''If 6&nbsp;builders can build 8&nbsp;houses in 100&nbsp;days, how many days would it take 10&nbsp;builders to build 20&nbsp;houses at the same rate?'', and this can be set up as

<math display="block">\frac{\frac{8\ \text{houses}}{100\ \text{days}}}{6\ \text{builders}} = \frac{\frac{20\ \text{houses}}{x}}{10\ \text{builders}},</math>

which, with cross-multiplication twice, gives

<math display="block"> x = \frac{20\ \text{houses} \times 100\ \text{days} \times 6\ \text{builders}}{8\ \text{houses} \times 10\ \text{builders}} = 150\ \text{days}.</math>

[[Lewis Carroll]]'s "[[The Mad Gardener's Song]]" includes the lines "He thought he saw a Garden-Door / That opened with a key: / He looked again, and found it was / A double Rule of Three".<ref>''[[Sylvie and Bruno]]'', Chapter 12.</ref>
